newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Sumitomo probes in U.S. grind on.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sumitomo probes in U.S. grind on.

text.p: One year on and U.S. probes and lawsuits linked to Sumitomo Corp's huge $2.6 billion loss from unauthorised copper dealings by its former star trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, appear far from resolution.

David Threlkeld, the trader who told the London Metal Exchange late 1991 of Hamanaka's request for confirmation of fictitious dealings, said another Sumitomo-type scandal could reoccur despite measures taken by the London exchange.

"What the London Metal Exchange requires is a revolution, a change in the ruling classes. It has done nothing to restore confidence in the market," Threlkeld said. "Not only do I believe it could happen again, it may well be happening."
Since the Sumitomo scandal broke, the LME has been taking steps to improve market transparency following a review by domestic regulatory watchdog the Securities and Investments Board.
LME has repeatedly said Sumitomo operated beyond its clutches in the over-the-counter and physical markets and took behind the scenes steps to alert the Japanese trade house of potential problems.
Copper prices are now back to the levels they were before the Sumitomo scandal broke and sent tags tumbling.

U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which began taking a closer look at the copper market in late 1996, several months before Sumitomo's massive loss was announced in June last year, said its probe was continuing.
"There is no deadline set - it's an on-going investigation," a CFTC spokesman said.
Privately officials close to U.S. regulators have said they look to financial watchdogs in London to take the lead in probing Sumitomo because they see Hamanaka's dealings linked to LME.
Nevertheless, blue chip banker J.P. Morgan & Co Inc was dealt a mild reprimand by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year for its role in financing Hamanaka's activities.

The U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan, which had subpoenaed Global Minerals and Metals for documents related to its dealings with Sumitomo and Hamanaka, reiterated it could neither confirm nor deny its probes.
The U.S. Attorney can help to gather information for government agencies such as the CFTC.

In April, a clutch of lawsuits, originally filed last year and alleging copper market rigging by Sumitomo and Global Minerals and Metals, a New York trading company, were rolled into one, beefed up with fresh evidence and refiled under seal.

The suit claimed that a key manipulation tool was a build-up of copper hoards in LME warehouses in Long Beach, Calif., whose opening in April 1995 the New York Mercantile's COMEX division, which also trades copper futures, criticized.
Hamanaka, on trial in Tokyo, has admitted to fraud and forgery charges, but Sumitomo has said there was no evidence of market rigging.
Global Minerals have always denied the charges in the lawsuits or any improper activities.
The lawsuits may have a hard time proving its case.

Earlier this month, Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairperson, Brooksley Born, told the International Derivatives Conference in London that every country had difficulty in deciding what is manipulation and how to act if it occurs.
"Manipulation is best prevented, rather than dealt with afterwards," Born said.

Meanwhile NYMEX executive vice president Neal Wolkoff said although Sumitomo was not a customer of the exchange, he would still like to see a better flow of information sharing between exchanges such as LME and NYMEX during a market crisis.
And he assumed more powers will be given by Congress to the CFTC to oversee and gather information about foreign exchanges that have delivery points in the U.S.
"These things are, to some extent, being addressed," Wolkoff said.
